the monomorphism restriction by 4.5.5's simple pattern binding (R18).
A restricted group's constrained variables stay open, and at the top
level are defaulted at the end of the module (R20), by the `default` of
the module their constraints arose in, refused where two modules'
differ, and refused where another module of the cycle fixes one (D30);
under `--cycle-default=scc`, by the group's one `default`, and closed at
the end of the group (an extension). Defaulting by 4.3.4's conditions
(R22).

members.name: env
members.doc:
What the checker knows of the program before a unit: the types of
its values, its type constructors, classes and instances.

members.name: initial
members.doc:
`initial {primitives}` is the environment with the built-in types and
constructors alone, and the values `primitives`.

Each primitive has the type `forall a. a`, until the overlay types
them (M17).

members.name: cycleDefault
members.doc: Where Rule 2 closes and which `default` holds in a cycle (D30).

members.name: module_
members.spec: type module_ = {id : string, ast : HsAst.module, library : bool}
members.doc:
A module of a unit: its identity, its renamed and resolved tree, and
whether it is the library's.

members.name: check
members.doc:
`check {env, unit, cycleDefault, prelude, fixity, evidence}` checks
the modules of `unit`, recording into `evidence`.

It gives the environment with the unit's types, constructors,
classes, instances and values, the errors, and the derived
instances' methods, made by HsDerive (M14), each with its module and
its instance's identity. `fixity key` is the fixity of the operator
of `key`, for a derived `Show` and `Read`. `prelude (space, name)` is
the key of the entity the Prelude exports under `name`, `"t"` for a
type or class and `"v"` for a value, for what the Report's
translations name: `Bool`, `Char`, `Integer`, `Double`, `Num`,
`Fractional`, `Eq`, `Ord`, `Enum`, `Integral`, `Monad`.

members.name: renumber
members.doc:
`renumber n` makes the checker's next fresh variables, and HsTypes',
number from `n`, where they have not passed it.

A program's are then numbered alike however much of the library was
checked before them (rhc's saved world, a program checked by
interfaces), and stay apart from each other and from the library's,
since a dictionary's name is one of them.

members.name: numberFrom
members.doc:
`numberFrom n` makes the checker's next fresh variables, and HsTypes',
number from `n`, whatever came before.

A unit given a range of its own is then numbered alike whatever was
checked before it: the library's units, which the saved world and a
whole program check in different numbers.

members.name: part
members.spec:
type part = {values : (string * HsTypes.scheme) list, tycons : HsKinds.tycon list, classes : HsClasses.class list,
             instances : HsClasses.instance list,
             cons : (string * {tycon : string, arity : int, fields : string list, strict : bool list}) list,
             fields : (string * {tycon : string, ty : HsTypes.ty, cons : (string * int) list}) list,
             methods : (string * {cls : string, scheme : HsTypes.scheme}) list}
members.doc:
What the environment holds of one module's entities, by key.

That is its values' types (its constructors', fields' and methods'
among them), its type constructors and synonyms, its classes, the
instances it declares or derives, and what the checker keeps of its
constructors, fields and methods. A unit's interface holds its
modules' parts (HsModIface, the haskell98 roadmap's M21).

members.name: part
members.doc:
`part (env, mine)` is what `env` holds of the entities whose module's
identity `mine` accepts, and of the instances it declares.

members.name: extend
members.doc:
`extend (env, p)` is `env` with the part `p`, as a client checks
against a module it has only the interface of.

members.name: setReaches
members.doc:
`setReaches f` makes `f (m, n)` the checker's answer to 5.4's scope.

`f (m, n)` is whether a chain of imports leads from the module `m` to
`n`, `m` among those it reaches: an instance is in scope in a module
only where it reaches the instance's (R26). The driver sets it from
the program's graph; until it does, every instance is in scope
everywhere.

members.name: valueScheme
members.spec: val valueScheme : env * string -> HsTypes.scheme option
members.doc: `valueScheme (env, key)` is the type of the value of `key`.

members.name: classes
members.doc: `classes env` is the classes and instances of `env`.

HS_KINDS.doc:
The type constructors of Haskell 98's checker and their kinds (the
haskell98 roadmap's M13; the Report's 4.6): kind inference over a
unit's `data`, `newtype`, `type` and `class` declarations by dependency
group, a kind left open defaulting to `*`, so that a type group may
cross the modules of a cycle (R28, D30); the kind checking of every
other type a program writes; and the types of the tree made the
checker's, synonyms expanded.

members.name: tycon
members.spec:
type tycon = {key : string, kind : HsTypes.kind, params : int, synonym : HsTypes.ty option,
              cons : string list, newtype : bool}
members.doc:
A type constructor: its key, its kind and the number of its
parameters.

With them, its right-hand side over `TGen 0` and on, for a synonym,
its constructors' keys, for `data` and `newtype`, and whether it is a
newtype.

members.name: env
members.doc: The type constructors of a program, by key.

members.name: find
members.spec: val find : env * string -> tycon option
members.doc:
`find (env, key)` is the type constructor of `key`, the built-in
ones among them.

members.name: keyOf
members.doc:
`keyOf n` is the key of the type constructor or class the name `n`
of the renamed tree stands for.

members.name: infer
members.spec:
val infer : {env : env, classKind : string -> HsTypes.kind option, decls : (string * HsAst.decl) list}
            -> {env : env, classKinds : (string * HsTypes.kind) list, errors : (HsSource.span * string) list}
members.doc:
`infer {env, classKind, decls}` infers the kinds of `decls`, the
type-level declarations of a unit, each with its module's identity.

It gives the environment with their type constructors, the kinds of
the unit's classes' variables, by the class's key, and the errors.
`classKind` gives the kind of a class of an earlier unit.

members.name: checkType
members.spec:
val checkType : {env : env, classKind : string -> HsTypes.kind option, vars : HsTypes.kind HsStringMap.map ref}
                -> HsAst.ty * HsTypes.kind -> unit
members.doc:
`checkType {env, classKind, vars} (t, want)` checks that the type `t`
is well kinded, of kind `want`.

Its variables' kinds are in `vars`, which it extends.

**Raises** `HsSource.Error` for a type ill kinded.

members.name: checkContext
members.spec:
val checkContext : {env : env, classKind : string -> HsTypes.kind option, vars : HsTypes.kind HsStringMap.map ref}
                   -> HsAst.ty option -> unit
members.doc:
`checkContext {env, classKind, vars} ctx` checks each class
assertion of the context `ctx`.

members.name: convert
members.spec: val convert : env * (string -> HsTypes.ty) -> HsAst.ty -> HsTypes.ty
members.doc:
`convert (env, var) t` is the type `t` as the checker's, its
variables by `var`.

Its synonyms are expanded.

**Raises** `HsSource.Error` for a synonym not applied to all its
parameters.

members.name: contextPreds
members.spec: val contextPreds : env * (string -> HsTypes.ty) -> HsAst.ty option -> HsTypes.pred list
members.doc: `contextPreds (env, var) ctx` is the predicates of a context.

members.name: tyVars
members.doc: `tyVars t` is the type variables of `t`, each once, in order.

HS_LAYOUT.doc:
The layout algorithm of Haskell 98, the function `L` of the Report's
section 9.3, run on demand: the parser pulls one token at a time, so
that when it takes an implicit close, the side condition
`parse-error(t)` of the equation for `t`, the stack of layout contexts
is that of the point it has reached and nothing past that token has
been laid out (the haskell98 roadmap's D27).

The equations and where they are kept:

- `<n>` with `m = n`, `n < m`, and otherwise: a token first on its line;
- `{n}` with `n > m`, `n > 0`, and otherwise: a token after `let`,
  `where`, `do` or `of` that is not `{`, and the first of a module that
  is neither `{` nor `module`; an empty block makes the next token's
  `{n}` an `<n>`;
- `}` with an explicit context on top, `{`, and the end of the input:
  `advance`;
- `t` with an implicit context on top and `parse-error(t)`:
  `closeImplicit`, which the parser calls.

It makes two readings of the roadmap's evidence (`results/E9/readings.md`):
R2, an explicit `}` may close an implicit block, as section 2.7 reads,
where 9.3's Note 3 alone would refuse it; and R3, a block opens only
at a column strictly greater than the enclosing one, so that a `do`
at the column of its context is empty.

There is one stream at a time: `start` begins it, and the parser reads
and moves it.

members.name: start
members.spec: val start : string * HsToken.item vector -> unit
members.doc:
`start (file, tokens)` begins the stream of the tokens of the file
`file`, laid out, and reads its first token.

members.name: current
members.doc: The token the stream is at, written or layout's.

members.name: here
members.doc:
`here ()` is the span of the current token; a token of layout's
covers no byte, and stands where the next written token begins.

members.name: currentStart
members.doc: `currentStart ()` is where the current token begins: `#start (here ())`.

members.name: trivia
members.doc:
`trivia ()` is the trivia before the current token; none for
layout's.

members.name: lastStop
members.doc:
`lastStop ()` is where the last written token that `advance` passed
ends: 0 before the first.

members.name: advance
members.doc:
`advance ()` passes the current token and reads the next.

**Raises** `HsSource.Error` for a `}` that no `{` opened, and for the
end of the input inside braces.

members.name: closeImplicit
members.doc:
`closeImplicit ()` is the equation of `t` with `parse-error(t)`: the
parser can go no further with the current token in its block.

Where that block is implicit it is closed and the result is `true`;
where it is explicit, or there is none, nothing changes and the
result is `false`.

members.name: peek
members.doc:
`peek k` is the `k`th written token after the current one, from 0,
as the lexer read it: layout does not see that far.

members.name: mark
members.doc: Where the stream is, to go back to.

members.name: save
members.doc: `save ()` is where the stream is now.

members.name: restore
members.doc: `restore m` puts the stream back where it was at `m`.

members.name: fail
members.doc:
`fail msg` raises an error at the current token.

**Raises** `HsSource.Error` always.

HS_LEXER.doc:
The lexer of Haskell 98: the Report's chapter 2 and section 9.2, over
program text.

The whole of a file becomes a vector of tokens before anything is
parsed, and nothing here depends on layout or on the parser, so that
this much of the language is a function of the text. Each token keeps
the trivia before it, and the end of the input keeps the trivia after
the last token, so that every byte of the text is in exactly one
token or one stretch of trivia.

The readings it makes, of `results/E9/readings.md` in the haskell98
roadmap's evidence:

- R4: the end of the file ends a line comment.
- R5: any character at all in a comment or a literal; identifiers and
  operators by the Report's classes (`HsChar`).
- R6: ASCII digits only in a numeric literal.
- R7: `F..` is the operator `.` qualified by `F`; `F.=` is `F` then
  `.=`; `M.where` is `M`, `.` and `where`; and, by the longest lexeme
  the text gives, `x F.-- y` is `x F.- - y` (R77), since `--` is dashes
  and no operator, and `x F.-> y` is `x F.- > y`.
- R8: `--:` is an operator; a numeric escape above 0x10FFFF is an
  error.
- A byte that is not part of a sequence of UTF-8 is read as the code
  point of its value, as Latin-1 would (the Report is silent on the
  bytes of a file).
- A byte order mark at the head of the file is trivia.

members.name: options
members.doc:
How to read: whether dotted module names are read.

`hierarchical` reads a dotted module name, such as Data.List, as one
qualifier, which Haskell 98's `modid` is not (the roadmap's D35,
refused by default).

members.name: defaults
members.doc: Haskell 98's: no dotted module names.

members.name: tokens
members.spec: val tokens : options * string * string -> HsToken.item vector
members.doc:
`tokens (options, file, text)` is the tokens of the program text
`text` of the file `file`, the last of them `EOF`.

**Raises** `HsSource.Error` for a lexical error: a character outside
the Report's classes, a literal or a nested comment left open, an
escape that is none.

HS_LINT.doc:
HsLint (the haskell98 roadmap's M16, D54): the independent check of
rhc's types, as AstLint is Rune's. Its first part is a second
inference: a transliteration of Typing Haskell in Haskell (Jones 1999)
in the form its 11.6.3 calls conformant, with kinds and dependency
groups recomputed, the monomorphism restriction and defaulting as the
roadmap's D32 reads the Report (R18, R20, R21, R22), over the renamed
tree. It shares nothing with rhc's checker but the renamer: its
unifier, its kinds and its context reduction are its own, so that a
disagreement between the two is a finding. rhc runs it among the
checks of level 2 (`--lint=2`, `RUNE_LINT=2`), where a refusal of a
program the compile accepts is a bug of rhc's.

members.name: module
members.spec: type module = {id : string, ast : HsAst.module, library : bool}
members.doc:
A module of a program as HsLint reads it: its identity, its tree as
`HsRename` renamed it and `HsFixity` resolved it, and whether it is
one of rhc's library's.

members.name: binding
members.spec:
type binding = {module : string, name : string, scheme : string, signed : bool, restricted : bool,
                span : HsSource.span}
members.doc:
A binding of the top level as the second inference left it: its
module, its name, its type as text, whether a signature declared it.

`restricted` is whether its group is restricted (4.5.5, Rule 1). The
type is written as the Report writes one, `Eq a => [a] -> a -> Bool`.

members.name: default
members.spec: type default = {module : string, span : HsSource.span, preds : string, choice : string, ruleTwo : bool}
members.doc:
A default the second inference chose (4.3.4): the module, where, the
predicates it resolved and the type, as text.

`ruleTwo` is whether Rule 2 chose it, where the module was inferred.

members.name: kind
members.spec: type kind = {module : string, name : string, kind : string}
members.doc:
The kind inferred for a type constructor or a class's variable (4.6):
the module, the name and the kind, as text.

members.name: class_
members.spec: type class_ = {name : string, numeric : bool, standard : bool}
members.doc: A class by its name: whether it is numeric and standard (4.3.4).

members.name: derived
members.doc:
A derived instance with the context inferred for it (4.3.3, 10.1):
the module of its type, and the instance as text, `Eq a => Eq (T a)`.

members.name: report
members.spec:
type report = {bindings : binding list, defaults : default list, kinds : kind list, derived : derived list,
               classes : class_ list}
members.doc:
What the second inference found: bindings, defaults, kinds, derived
instances and classes.

The bindings of the top level of every module and the defaults are in
the order it met them; the kinds are of the type constructors and the
classes.

members.name: Refused
members.doc:
A refusal of the second inference: where, and why, the why naming the
row of the conformance table it is for where there is one.

members.name: infer
members.spec: val infer : {groups : module list list, main : string option, cycleDefault : bool} -> report
members.doc:
`infer {groups, main, cycleDefault}` is the report of the second
inference over the program whose groups of modules are `groups`.

The groups are the strongly connected ones, dependencies first;
`main` is the identity of the module whose `main` must have the type
`IO t` (5), if any; and `cycleDefault` is whether a group's modules
share one `default` and Rule 2 closes at the group's end (D30's
`--cycle-default=scc`) rather than each module's.

**Raises** `Refused` at the first breach of the Report's static rules
the second inference finds.

members.name: claims
members.doc:
What a record claims of a program, in the form `dump` prints.

The claims are kinds, derived instances, the types of the bindings of
its modules' top levels and the defaults.

members.name: claims
members.doc:
`claims text` is the claims of `text`, lines in the form of `dump`;
a line of another form claims nothing.

members.name: rules
members.doc:
`rules` is each rule of `compare` with what it holds, its name being
the first word of its breach's message, in brackets: `[rule1] ...`.

members.name: compare
members.spec: val compare : report * claims * (HsSource.span -> string) * string -> unit
members.doc:
`compare (report, claims, where_, fault)` holds the claims to the
report, of the program's modules, `where_` giving a default's place.

`fault`, a rule's name or "", reads the first claim that rule checks
corrupted, so that the rule must refuse it.

**Raises** `Refused` at the first claim a rule refuses.

members.name: replayRules
members.doc:
`replayRules` is each rule of replay with what it holds (Faxén's
rules and rhc's), its name the first word of its breach's message, in
brackets: `[bindg] ...`.

members.name: target
members.doc:
What the second inference found that the target check reads.

They are the types of the top level, the selectors and default
methods, the classes' dictionaries and the instances' dictionary
functions, as Core's types.

members.name: library
members.doc:
HsLint's part of a unit: what one check inferred alone.

It is the environment's entries of the modules it inferred, what their
inference found and the target check's data of them: a saved world's
library, or a unit's in the store, from which the modules after it are
inferred alone (D45).

members.name: check
members.doc:
`check {groups, main, cycleDefault, records, claims, where_, fault, library}` is `infer`'s report, with the checker's records replayed and
compared.

With `library`, the groups of its modules are not inferred again: the
rest are inferred after its environment and findings, and only the
records of those modules are replayed, the library's having been
replayed where it was inferred. The report is of the modules inferred,
and `part` what was inferred of them alone, for the units after them.

It gives what the target check reads with the report. With `records`,
the checker's evidence records and environment (HsEvidence, HsInfer) and the derived instances it made as trees
(HsDerive: each one's module, identity and methods), the second
inference checks those instances' methods as any instance's, each
record is replayed by Faxén's rules and rhc's (`replayRules`), the
derived methods' records too, and the records are then held to the
inference as claims (`compare`); with `claims`, those are too.
`fault` is as `compare`'s, for every rule.

**Raises** `Refused` at the first breach.

members.name: join
members.doc:
`join parts` is the parts of units put together, in order: a later
part's entry of a name wins, and the rest are appended.

members.name: Decode
members.doc: Bytes that are no part of a unit, and why.

members.name: encode
members.doc: `encode part` is `part` as bytes, in Pickle's form.

members.name: decode
members.doc:
`decode bytes` is the part `bytes` are, as `encode` wrote it.

**Raises** `Decode` where the bytes are no part.

members.name: targetRules
members.doc:
`targetRules` is each rule of the target check with what it holds,
its name the first word of its breach's message, in brackets:
`[target] ...`.

members.name: target
members.spec: val target : target * Core.program * string -> unit
members.doc:
`target (t, program, fault)` holds `program`, the Core made of what
`check` read, to `t`, what the second inference found.

The program is what desugaring made and CoreLint accepted. Each value
of the top level, selector and default method, each class's
dictionary and each instance's dictionary function is held to the
translation of its source type, as the second inference has it (Hall
et al.'s soundness of the translation), up to the names and order of
its variables and the order of its dictionaries. `fault` is as
`compare`'s.

**Raises** `Refused` at the first breach.

members.name: dump
members.spec: val dump : report * (HsSource.span -> string) * bool -> string
members.doc:
`dump (report, where_, library)` is the report as text, a line each.

The lines are `KIND MODULE NAME :: KIND` for a type constructor or a
class, `DERIVED MODULE INSTANCE`, `TYPE MODULE NAME :: TYPE` for a
binding, `SIGNED` for one with a signature, and `DEFAULT MODULE WHERE PREDS -> TYPE`, where `where_` gives a span's place: of the program's
modules, and of the library's too where `library` is set, but its
signed bindings, and its defaults at no place, `*`. The lines of each
kind are sorted by module, then name, instance or place, so that only
a change of what one says moves the dump.

HS_LITERATE.doc:
Literate Haskell (the Report's section 9.4): the program text of a
literate file.

The program text has the length of the file, byte for byte, so that a
position of the one is a position of the other: a program line keeps
its bytes but for its leading `>`, which becomes a space, so that its
columns are the file's, and every byte of a line of commentary but its
line end becomes a space. Layout sees no line of commentary, and the
trivia that an exact print takes from the file keep it.

members.name: isLiterate
members.doc:
`isLiterate name` is whether `name` is that of a literate file: it
ends in `.lhs`.

members.name: unlit
members.doc:
`unlit (file, bytes)` is the program text of the literate file
`file`, whose bytes are `bytes`.

A line that begins with `>` is a program line, and so is every line
between a line that begins with `\begin{code}` and one that begins
with `\end{code}`; every other line is commentary.

**Raises** `HsSource.Error` for a program line next to a line of
commentary that is not blank, for a `\begin{code}` that no
`\end{code}` closes, and for an `\end{code}` that no `\begin{code}`
opened.

HS_MATCH.doc:
Pattern matching in the Report's order (the haskell98 roadmap's M15,
D34), and decision trees in Sestoft's order as an option.

The rules of 3.17.3 are taken literally, at `-O0`; the trees are built
for D34's measurement.

The Report's order: the clauses one after another, and in each the
patterns from left to right, each from the outside in (3.17.2). A
clause that fails goes to the next, which a lazy `let` of the rest of
the match holds (rule (c)'s `y`), so no clause is copied (defect 14).
A constructor's pattern forces its value and matches its fields left
to right (rule (g)); a newtype's casts and forces nothing (rules (k),
(l)); a numeric literal compares by `==` at its type with the
dictionaries the checker chose (rule (h)), a character literal by a
case on its code point, a string literal as the list of its characters
(defect 7); `~p` binds each variable of `p` to a match of its own that
is made only when the variable is forced (rule (d)); `x@p` binds `x`
to the value (rule (e)); `n+k` compares by `>=` and binds `n` to the
value less `k` (rule (s)); a record pattern tests its constructor and
matches its fields in the pattern's order (rules (m) to (o)).

Sestoft's order (Sestoft 1996) matches the same patterns in the same
order, but makes no test whose outcome the tests made already decide:
a decision tree whose right-hand sides are functions of their
variables, so that none is copied. Its only freedom is in tests on
values already forced (D34). A clause with a pattern it does not take
apart (a literal, `~p`, `n+k`, a newtype's or a record's) is matched
from there on in the Report's way.

members.name: order
members.doc: How clauses are matched.

members.name: order
members.doc:
`order` is the order of every match: `Report`, `-O0`'s, unless rhc is
told otherwise.

members.name: occurrence
members.doc: What is matched: an atom of Core and its type.

members.name: clause
members.spec: type clause = HsAst.pat list * (HsDsEnv.env * HsDsCore.texp -> HsDsCore.texp)
members.doc:
A clause: its patterns, and its right-hand side, made in the scope of
the patterns' variables and given what to do where its guards all
fail.

members.name: clauses
members.spec: val clauses : HsDsEnv.env * occurrence list * clause list * (Core.ty -> HsDsCore.texp) -> HsDsCore.texp
members.doc:
`clauses (env, occurrences, rows, failure)` matches the occurrences
against each clause of `rows` in turn.

Each pattern is matched against its occurrence; the match is the
right-hand side of the first clause that matches, or `failure t` where
none does, `t` the type of the match.

members.name: pattern
members.spec:
val pattern : HsDsEnv.env * occurrence * HsAst.pat * (HsDsEnv.env -> HsDsCore.texp) * HsDsCore.texp
              -> HsDsCore.texp
members.doc:
`pattern (env, occurrence, p, success, failure)` matches one
occurrence against `p` in the Report's way.

It is `success` in the scope of `p`'s variables where it matches, and
`failure`, an atom, where it does not.

members.name: variables
members.doc:
`variables p` is the variables `p` binds, in order, by their names in
the renamed tree.

members.name: lazy
members.doc:
`lazy p` is whether `p` never fails and forces nothing: a variable,
`_`, `~p` and `x@p` of one of these.

HS_MODULES.doc:
The names of Haskell 98's modules (the Report's chapter 5; the haskell98
roadmap's D29, D30): what each module defines, what it exports, and what
is in scope in it, over a group of modules that import one another.

An entity is a thing a name can stand for: its name space, the module
that defines it, by that module's identity, and its name. A name stands
for zero, one or several entities, and is an error only where it is used
and stands for other than one, in the manner of Diatchki, Jones and
Hallgren 2002. Within a strongly connected group of modules the exports
and the scopes are defined by each other, and are solved by iteration:
from nothing, the least fixpoint (D29's A, the default), or from
everything, the greatest. Instances are not names, and every instance a
program declares is visible in all of it.

members.name: space
members.doc:
The two name spaces: values (variables, constructors, fields,
methods) and types (type constructors, synonyms, classes).

members.name: entity
members.spec: type entity = {space : space, home : string, name : string}
members.doc:
An entity: its space, the identity of the module that defines it, and
its name.

A module's identity is its name for a module of the program, and its
library's name, a colon and its name for a library's: a program's
`Char` is not the library's.

members.name: key
members.doc: `key e` is `e` as a string, unique to it, for maps and sets.

members.name: moduleName
members.doc:
`moduleName id` is the name of the module of identity `id`, without
its library.

members.name: sort
members.spec:
datatype sort =
    Var
  | Con
  | Field
  | Method
  | TyCon
  | Synonym
  | Class
members.doc: What a top-level definition is.

members.name: def
members.spec: type def = {entity : entity, sort : sort, parent : entity option, arity : int, span : HsSource.span}
members.doc:
A top-level definition: its entity, what it is, and where it is.

With them, the type or class it belongs to, for a constructor, a field
or a method, and the number of arguments a constructor takes.

members.name: defs
members.spec: val defs : string * HsAst.module -> def list
members.doc:
`defs (id, m)` is what the module `m` of identity `id` defines at its
top level, each once, in the order of the source.

members.name: unit_
members.spec: type unit_ = {id : string, name : string, ast : HsAst.module, imports : (HsAst.import * string) list}
members.doc:
A module as resolution reads it: its identity, its name, its tree,
and its imports.

Each import has the identity of the module it names, the implicit
import of the Prelude among them where the module has one.

members.name: scope
members.doc:
What is in scope in a module: the entities a name stands for, by
`scopeKey`.

members.name: scopeKey
members.spec: val scopeKey : space * string * string -> string
members.doc:
`scopeKey (space, qual, name)` is the key of the name `name` qualified
by `qual`, `""` for none, in the space `space`.

members.name: lookup
members.spec: val lookup : scope * space * string * string -> entity list
members.doc:
`lookup (scope, space, qual, name)` is the entities the name stands
for: none, one, or several.

members.name: fixpoint
members.doc: The fixpoint to take where a group's exports admit several.

members.name: solved
members.spec:
type solved = {exports : entity list HsStringMap.map, scopes : scope HsStringMap.map,
               errors : (HsSource.span * string) list}
members.doc:
What `solve` makes of a group: each module's exports and scope, by
identity, and the errors of the group's export and import lists.

members.name: solve
members.spec:
val solve : {group : unit_ list, exportsOf : string -> entity list, defOf : string -> def option,
             universe : entity list, fixpoint : fixpoint} -> solved
members.doc:
`solve {group, exportsOf, defOf, universe, fixpoint}` solves the
exports and the scopes of the strongly connected group of modules
`group`.

`exportsOf id` gives the exports of a module outside the group,
solved before it, `defOf` gives the definition of every entity of the
program, by `key`, and `universe` is every entity of the program,
from which the greatest fixpoint starts. The errors are
those of chapter 5: an export of what is not in scope, of a module
that is not imported, two entities exported under one name, an import
of what a module does not export.

HS_MOD_IFACE.doc:
A module's interface as the renamer and the checker make it (the
haskell98 roadmap's M21, D44): what a client of the module needs of it
to be named and checked against it in place of its source, by entity,
and the fingerprints a store's usages compare (E13's H5, H6). HsIface,
rhc's interface of a unit, holds one for each of its modules beside its
Core, and codes them.

members.name: t
members.spec:
type t = {id : string, exports : HsModules.entity list, defs : HsModules.def list,
          fixities : (string * (HsAst.fixity * int)) list, checked : HsInfer.part}
members.doc:
A module's interface, what a client is named and checked by.

It holds the module's identity; what it exports, by entity, as
HsModules solved them; what it defines at its top level, with its
sort, parent and arity, which an import of `T(..)` reads; the
fixities of its operators, by entity key; and its part of the
checker's environment.

members.name: make
members.spec:
val make : {id : string, exports : HsModules.entity list, defs : HsModules.def list,
            fixity : string -> (HsAst.fixity * int) option, env : HsInfer.env} -> t
members.doc:
`make {id, exports, defs, fixity, env}` is the interface of the module
`id`, from the program's tables after its unit is checked.

`fixity key` is the fixity of an operator, and `env` the checker's
environment.

members.name: canonical
members.doc:
`canonical t` is each item of the interface by its key, with the text
that stands for what a client reads of it.

An item is a type with its constructors and fields, a class with its
methods, a value, or an instance by its identity; its text holds keys,
kinds, schemes over `TGen` numbers, contexts, and the fixities of its
names. Two interfaces that a client reads alike have the same text.

members.name: fingerprints
members.spec: val fingerprints : (string -> string) -> t list * (string -> string option) -> (string * string) list
members.doc:
`fingerprints hash (ts, external)` is the fingerprint of each entity
and instance of the modules `ts`, by its key or identity.

The modules are those of one unit, an SCC of the module graph, taken
together. A type's constructors and fields and a class's methods have their
parent's.

Items are taken in recursive groups (one mentions another, through a
type, a class, a superclass, an instance's class, type or context),
over all of `ts`, so that a group that spans the modules of a cycle is
one (H8): a group's fingerprint is `hash` of its members' canonical
text and of the fingerprints of the entities outside `ts` they
mention, `external key` (the key itself where that is NONE: a
built-in type), so that it moves where what a client reads of it
moves, and with what it mentions.

HS_PARSER.doc:
The parser of Haskell 98: recursive descent over the grammar of the
Report's section 9.5, on the layout of `HsLayout` (the haskell98
roadmap's D27).

A block's item parser returns as soon as the next token cannot go on
with the item, so a block that then sees neither `;` nor its close is
at `parse-error(t)`, and takes the implicit close there; nothing else
here knows of layout. Operators stay in flat sequences, so no fixity is
needed (R1: `do a == b == c` parses, and fixity resolution refuses it).
A declaration's left-hand side and a statement's pattern are read as
relaxed patterns and checked once the token after them says what they
are.

members.name: annotations
members.doc:
How much of the source a tree keeps.

`Bare`, none, so that two trees compare equal where they differ only
in where they were read; `Spans`, a span on every node; `Full`, spans
and every node's own tokens with their trivia, which `HsPrint.exact`
needs.

members.name: options
members.doc: How to read: the lexer's options, and the annotations.

members.name: defaults
members.doc: Haskell 98's lexer, and `Full` annotations.

members.name: parse
members.spec: val parse : options * string * HsToken.item vector -> HsAst.module
members.doc:
`parse (options, file, tokens)` is the module the tokens of the file
`file` hold.

**Raises** `HsSource.Error` at the first syntax error.

members.name: parseTraced
members.spec: val parseTraced : options * string * HsToken.item vector -> HsAst.module * HsToken.token list
members.doc:
`parseTraced (options, file, tokens)` is `parse`'s module, and every
token the parser passed, in order.

The braces and semicolons of layout are as layout gave them: the
function `L` of section 9.3, on the source.

**Raises** `HsSource.Error` at the first syntax error.

members.name: parseFile
members.spec: val parseFile : options * string * string -> HsAst.module
members.doc:
`parseFile (options, file, bytes)` is the module that the file
`file`, whose bytes are `bytes`, holds.

It is unlit first where its name is a literate file's (`HsLiterate`),
then lexed and parsed.

**Raises** `HsSource.Error` at the first error.

HS_PRINT.doc:
Printers of Haskell 98's abstract syntax (the haskell98 roadmap's D28).

Three prints share one walk of the tree. `explicit` writes every block
in braces with semicolons, so that no layout rule applies to what it
writes; `implicit` writes every block by layout, each item on a line of
its own; both print every token a node stands for and nothing else, so
that reading a print back gives the tree printed, and its tokens are
those of `L` of the source but for empty items and a trailing comma
(the tree and token round trips of the roadmap's section Round trips).
`exact` prints a tree read with `Full` annotations as its file, byte for
byte: every token where the source had it, with the comments, pragmas
and white space before it. A node with no annotation, which a tool made,
is printed by `exact` as `explicit` prints it.

members.name: explicit
members.doc: `explicit m` is `m` with every block in braces.

members.name: implicit
members.doc:
`implicit m` is `m` with every block by layout, but an empty one,
which is `{}`.

members.name: exact
members.doc:
`exact (bytes, m)` is the file whose bytes, `bytes`, `m` was read
from with `Full` annotations; for a tree a tool changed, the file with
the change.

members.name: exp
members.doc:
`exp e`, `pat p`, `ty t` and `decl d` are nodes as `explicit` prints
them, for a message.

members.name: pat
members.doc:
`exp e`, `pat p`, `ty t` and `decl d` are nodes as `explicit` prints
them, for a message.

members.name: ty
members.doc:
`exp e`, `pat p`, `ty t` and `decl d` are nodes as `explicit` prints
them, for a message.

members.name: decl
members.doc:
`exp e`, `pat p`, `ty t` and `decl d` are nodes as `explicit` prints
them, for a message.

HS_RENAME.doc:
Haskell 98's renamer (the haskell98 roadmap's M12): every name of a
module's tree resolved to what it stands for, in the scope that
`HsModules` gives the module and the scopes its own bindings make.

The renamed tree is a tree of `HsAst`, with every name rewritten: a name
of the top level is its entity, qualified by the identity of the module
that defines it (`{qual = home, name = name}`), and a local one, a
variable a pattern or a local declaration binds, is unqualified and made
unique with a `#` and a number, which no name of the source can hold.
Type variables and the built-in names (`()`, `[]`, `:`, the tuples',
`(->)`) stay as they are written. The static checks that need names
are made here: a name in scope, and standing for one entity; a
constructor applied to as many patterns as it takes; one definition of a
name in a group of bindings, its clauses together; a signature or a
fixity declaration only for what its group defines; an instance's method
one of its class's.

members.name: fixity
members.doc: The associativity and the precedence of an operator.

members.name: renamed
members.spec:
type renamed = {module : HsAst.module, localFixities : fixity HsStringMap.map,
                errors : (HsSource.span * string) list}
members.doc:
What a module's renaming gives: the tree, the fixities declared for
its local operators, by their unique names, and the errors, in the
order of the source.

members.name: rename
members.spec:
val rename : {id : string, scope : HsModules.scope, defOf : string -> HsModules.def option}
             -> HsAst.module -> renamed
members.doc:
`rename {id, scope, defOf} m` renames the module `m` of identity
`id`, whose scope is `scope`.

`defOf` gives the definition of every entity of the program by
`HsModules.key`.

members.name: topFixities
members.spec: val topFixities : string * HsAst.module -> (string * fixity) list
members.doc:
`topFixities (id, m)` is the fixities that the module `m` of identity
`id` declares at its top level and in its classes, by the key of the
operator's entity.

HS_SCC.doc:
Strongly connected components, for the dependency analyses of Haskell
98's checker: of type declarations for kinds (4.6), and of bindings for
declaration groups (4.5.1).

members.name: sccs
members.spec: val sccs : string list * (string -> string list) -> string list list
members.doc:
`sccs (nodes, edges)` is the components of the graph of `nodes`, each
after every one it depends on.

`edges n` is the nodes `n` depends on, those not among `nodes`
ignored; a component's members are in the order of `nodes`.

HS_SOURCE.doc:
Haskell source text: spans, positions and the errors of the front end.

A position is a byte offset of the file everywhere inside the front end,
as it is inside Rune's compiler (docs/diagnostics.md, Columns), and a
span is the compiler's span, as lib/compiler's Source has it, so that a
driver can show a diagnostic of `lib/language/haskell` as it shows its own. A line and a
column are worked out only where a diagnostic is shown.

members.name: span
members.spec: type span = {file : string, start : int, stop : int}
members.doc: The bytes from `start` up to `stop` of the file named `file`.

members.name: noSpan
members.doc:
The span of no text, for a node that a tool made rather than the
parser read.

members.name: join
members.doc:
`join (a, b)` is the span from the first byte of either to the last
of either; the file is `a`'s.

members.name: text
members.doc: A file's name and bytes, with where each of its lines begins.

members.name: text
members.spec: val text : {file : string, bytes : string} -> text
members.doc: `text {file, bytes}` is the text of a file, with its table of lines.

members.name: file
members.doc: `file t` is the name `t` was made with.

members.name: bytes
members.doc: `bytes t` is the bytes `t` was made with.

members.name: position
members.spec: val position : text * int -> {line : int, column : int}
members.doc:
`position (t, offset)` is the line of the byte `offset`, from 1, and
its column, from 1, counting the characters before it on its line.

A code point of UTF-8 counts one, and so does a byte that is not
UTF-8. A tab counts one, as rustc and Emacs count
(docs/diagnostics.md).

members.name: Error
members.doc:
An error of the front end: where, and what, in a message that starts
lowercase and names the construct.

members.name: message
members.spec: val message : text * span * string -> string
members.doc:
`message (t, span, msg)` is the first line of a diagnostic, as Rune's
compiler prints it.

It is `FILE:LINE:COL: error: MESSAGE`, where `FILE` has its control
characters escaped as `\u{1B}`.

HS_STRING_MAP.doc:
Maps keyed by strings, as the front end's scopes, exports and tables
need them: persistent, ordered by the keys, and balanced (red-black
trees, inserting only), so that a fold visits the keys in order and a
result does not depend on the order things were added.

members.name: map
members.doc: A map from strings to values of type `'a`.

members.name: empty
members.doc: The map with no key.

members.name: insert
members.doc:
`insert (m, k, v)` is `m` with `k` mapped to `v`, in place of what `m`
mapped it to.

members.name: find
members.doc: `find (m, k)` is what `m` maps `k` to, if anything.

members.name: member
members.doc: `member (m, k)` is whether `m` maps `k`.

members.name: foldl
members.doc:
`foldl f init m` folds `f` over the keys and values of `m` in the
order of the keys.

members.name: listItems
members.doc: `listItems m` is the pairs of `m` in the order of the keys.

members.name: size
members.doc: `size m` is the number of keys of `m`.

HS_TOKEN.doc:
The lexemes of Haskell 98 (the Report's chapter 2 and section 9.2), with
what lies between them.

Three tokens are the layout algorithm's (section 9.3) and never the
lexer's: `VLBRACE`, `VSEMI` and `VRBRACE`, the braces and semicolon it
puts in. They stay apart from the written ones, so that a trace shows
what layout did. Comments, pragmas and white space are not tokens: each
token keeps the trivia before it, so that a tree can be printed back as
its file (the haskell98 roadmap's D28).

members.name: token
members.spec:
datatype token =
    VARID of string
  | CONID of string
  | QVARID of string * string
  | QCONID of string * string
  | VARSYM of string
  | CONSYM of string
  | QVARSYM of string * string
  | QCONSYM of string * string
  | INTEGER of IntInf.int * string
  | FLOAT of string
  | CHAR of int * string
  | STRING of int list * string
  | LPAREN | RPAREN | COMMA | SEMI | LBRACKET | RBRACKET | BACKQUOTE | LBRACE
  | RBRACE
  | DOTDOT | COLON | DCOLON | EQUALS | BACKSLASH | BAR | LARROW | RARROW | AT | TILDE
  | DARROW
  | CASE | CLASS | DATA | DEFAULT | DERIVING | DO | ELSE | IF | IMPORT | IN | INFIX
  | INFIXL | INFIXR | INSTANCE | LET | MODULE | NEWTYPE | OF | THEN | TYPE | WHERE
  | UNDERSCORE
  | VLBRACE
  | VSEMI
  | VRBRACE
  | EOF
members.doc:
A lexeme. A qualified name is its qualifier and its name; a literal
keeps its value and its text as written.

members.name: trivia
members.spec:
datatype trivia =
    Whitespace
  | LineComment
  | BlockComment
  | Pragma
  | ByteOrderMark
members.doc: What a stretch of trivia is.

members.name: trivium
members.spec: type trivium = {kind : trivia, start : int, stop : int}
members.doc: A stretch of trivia, by the bytes of the file it covers.

members.name: item
members.spec:
type item = {token : token, start : int, stop : int, line : int, column : int, first : bool,
             trivia : trivium list}
members.doc:
A token as the lexer reads it, with where it is.

The bytes it covers, the line it is on, its column as layout counts
it (a tab to the next multiple of eight, plus one), whether it is the
first token of its line, and the trivia before it.

members.name: reservedId
members.doc: `reservedId s` is the keyword `s` is, if it is one; `_` among them.

members.name: reservedOp
members.doc: `reservedOp s` is the reserved operator `s` is, if it is one.

members.name: show
members.doc:
`show t` is the text `t` stands for, `{v`, `v;` and `v}` for layout's
tokens and `<eof>` for the end.

members.name: describe
members.doc:
`describe t` names `t` in a diagnostic: its text in backquotes, and
layout's tokens and the end by what they are.

members.name: plain
members.doc:
`plain t` is the written token that layout's `t` stands for, and `t`
when it is not layout's.

HS_TYPES.doc:
The types of Haskell 98's checker (the haskell98 roadmap's M13, D31):
kinds, types with unification variables, predicates and schemes, and
first-order unification with levels.

A type constructor is named by the key of its entity (`HsModules.key`),
or is one of the built-in ones, named as the renamer leaves them: `()`,
`[]`, `->`, and the tuples' `(,)`, `(,,)` and on. A unification
variable is a cell, linked once it is solved; its level is the depth of
the binding group that made it, so that generalisation takes the
variables deeper than the group's level, and its home is the module
whose code made it, which Rule 2 in a cycle reads (D30). A variable of a
signature or of an instance head, fixed while it is checked, is rigid.

members.name: kind
members.spec: datatype kind = KStar | KFun of kind * kind | KVar of kvar ref
members.doc: A kind, with variables that kind inference solves.

members.name: kvar
members.spec: datatype kvar = KFree of int | KLink of kind
members.doc: A kind variable: unsolved, by its number, or linked to a kind.

members.name: newKind
members.doc: `newKind ()` is a fresh kind variable.

members.name: kindRepr
members.doc: `kindRepr k` follows the links of `k`'s variable, if it has one.

members.name: defaultKind
members.doc: `defaultKind k` is `k` with every unsolved variable made `*`.

members.name: showKind
members.doc: `showKind k` is `k` as the Report writes one.

members.name: KindMismatch
members.doc: Two kinds that cannot be one.

members.name: unifyKind
members.doc:
`unifyKind (a, b)` makes `a` and `b` one kind.

**Raises** `KindMismatch` where they cannot be.

members.name: rigid
members.doc: A rigid variable: a number for itself and its name as written.

members.name: ty
members.spec:
datatype ty =
    TCon of string
  | TAp of ty * ty
  | TMeta of meta ref
  | TGen of int
  | TRigid of rigid
members.doc: A type. `TGen i` is the `i`th variable a scheme binds.

members.name: meta
members.doc:
A unification variable: unsolved, with its number, its level and its
home module, or linked to the type it was solved as.

members.name: pred
members.doc: A predicate, `C t`: a class, by the key of its entity, and a type.

members.name: scheme
members.spec: type scheme = {vars : int, ctx : pred list, ty : ty}
members.doc:
A scheme: the number of variables it binds, its context and its type,
over `TGen 0` to `TGen (vars - 1)`.

members.name: unitCon
members.doc: The unit's type constructor, `()`.

members.name: listCon
members.doc: The list's type constructor, `[]`.

members.name: arrowCon
members.doc: The function's type constructor, `->`.

members.name: tupleCon
members.doc: `tupleCon n` is the type constructor of the tuples of `n` components.

members.name: builtinKind
members.doc: `builtinKind name` is the kind of a built-in type constructor.

members.name: fn_
members.doc: `fn_ (a, b)` is the type `a -> b`.

members.name: list
members.doc: `list t` is the type `[t]`.

members.name: tuple
members.doc: `tuple ts` is the tuple of the types `ts`.

members.name: unit
members.doc: The unit's type, `()`.

members.name: apply
members.spec: val apply : ty * ty list -> ty
members.doc: `apply (t, args)` is `t` applied to `args`, left to right.

members.name: spine
members.spec: val spine : ty -> ty * ty list
members.doc: `spine t` is the head of `t` and its arguments.

members.name: newMeta
members.doc: `newMeta (level, home)` is a fresh unification variable.

members.name: renumber
members.doc:
`renumber n` makes the next fresh unification and kind variables
number from `n`, where they have not passed it.

What follows is then numbered alike however much came before it below
`n` (rhc's saved world, a program checked by interfaces).

members.name: numberFrom
members.doc:
`numberFrom n` makes the next fresh unification and kind variables
number from `n`, whatever came before.

The caller sees that no variable it numbered at or past `n` stands.

members.name: repr
members.doc: `repr t` follows `t`'s links to its head.

members.name: zonk
members.doc: `zonk t` is `t` with every solved variable replaced, through.

members.name: metas
members.spec: val metas : ty -> meta ref list
members.doc: `metas t` is the unsolved variables of `t`, each once, in order.

members.name: metaId
members.doc: `metaId m` is the number of an unsolved variable.

members.name: metaLevel
members.doc: `metaLevel m` is the level of an unsolved variable.

members.name: metaHome
members.doc: `metaHome m` is the module whose code made an unsolved variable.

members.name: setLevel
members.spec: val setLevel : meta ref * int -> unit
members.doc: `setLevel (m, l)` moves an unsolved variable to the level `l`.

members.name: Mismatch
members.doc: Two types that differ, which unification cannot make one.

members.name: Occurs
members.doc: A variable that occurs in the type unification would make it.

members.name: unify
members.spec: val unify : (meta ref * ty -> unit) -> ty * ty -> unit
members.doc:
`unify watch (a, b)` makes `a` and `b` one type, solving variables.

On each variable it solves, `watch` is told it and the type.

**Raises** `Mismatch` where the types differ, and `Occurs` where a
variable would contain itself.

members.name: instantiate
members.spec: val instantiate : scheme * int * string -> ty list * pred list * ty
members.doc:
`instantiate (s, level, home)` is `s`'s type and context with fresh
variables for its own, and those variables.

members.name: substGen
members.spec: val substGen : ty list * ty -> ty
members.doc: `substGen (ts, t)` replaces `TGen i` by the `i`th of `ts`.

members.name: nameOfKey
members.doc:
`nameOfKey k` is the name of the entity of key `k`, as a message shows
it; a built-in name is itself.

members.name: show
members.doc:
`show t` is `t` as Haskell writes it.

Its unsolved variables are named `t1`, `t2` and on by their numbers,
a rigid variable by its name as written.

members.name: showPred
members.doc: `showPred p` is the predicate `p` as a context writes it.

members.name: showScheme
members.doc:
`showScheme s` is the scheme `s` as a signature writes it, its
variables `a`, `b` and on.

HS_USAGE.doc:
What a compile of a unit reads of the units it imports (the haskell98
roadmap's M21, E13's obligations H1, H2, H7 and H9), noted where the
renamer, the checker and the translations read it, so that a store's
entry of the unit is used only where each read gives now what it gave
then. A read is noted found or not: a name a module looks up and does
not find is read too, since an import that comes to export it changes
the module (5.5.2). The note is a no-op until a driver sets it (rhc's,
src/rhc/iface.sml).

members.name: read
members.doc:
A read. Spaces are `"v"` for a value and `"t"` for a type or class,
and entities, classes and type constructors are by their keys
(HsModules.key).

members.name: setNote
members.doc:
`setNote f` makes `f` the recorder, called with each read as it is
made, and is the recorder before it: until a driver sets one, a no-op.

members.name: read
members.doc: `read r` notes `r`.

members.name: key
members.doc:
`key r` is `r` as one line of text, its fields apart by spaces, the
name of a store's usage.

**Example** `key (Exports "M") = "exports M"`

members.name: fromKey
members.doc: `fromKey s` is the read whose key is `s`, NONE for none.
